n: The narrator introduces Boaz before Ruth meets him: a relative of Elimelech and a man of wealth and standing. The reader now knows something Ruth does not.

f.g: A relative in the clan who could have duties to help family in need.
The Hebrew can mean wealthy, capable, or of strong character — Boaz is all three.

n: Ruth takes the initiative to support Naomi by gleaning, hoping to find a landowner who will be kind to a foreigner. Naomi gives her blessing.

f.g: To gather leftover grain the harvesters missed. God's law required farmers to leave these for the poor, foreigners, widows, and orphans.
In KJV English, “corn” means grain in general — here, barley.

n: Ruth “happens” to land in the field of Boaz. The narrator's understatement invites readers to see God's quiet guidance in what looks like chance.

f.w: her hap was to light on
f.g: As it happened, she came upon — a gentle hint of providence.

n: Boaz greets his workers in the Lord's name and they bless him in return. This small exchange shows a godly, respectful workplace.
Boaz notices the stranger among the gleaners and asks his foreman who she belongs to — that is, whose family she is part of.

f.g: young woman

n: The foreman identifies her by her foreign origin: the Moabite woman who returned with Naomi. Word of Ruth had already spread in the small town.
The foreman reports that Ruth asked permission politely and has worked hard since morning with only a short rest. Her diligence matches her loyalty.

f.g: stayed, rested

n: Boaz speaks to Ruth tenderly, calling her “my daughter” (he is likely older). He invites her to stay in his field with his young women, where she will be safe.

f.g: stay close beside

n: Boaz protects Ruth from harassment by ordering the young men not to bother her, and gives her access to the water the workers drew — generous treatment for a gleaner.

f.g: thirsty
Here, to bother, harm, or harass.

n: Ruth bows to the ground in deep gratitude, amazed that he would notice and care for a foreigner like her.

f.g: notice me, pay attention to me. In Hebrew this sounds like the word for “foreigner,” a wordplay.
foreigner, outsider

n: Boaz explains that he has heard all about her kindness to Naomi and her courage in leaving her homeland. Like Abraham, she left family and country to come to a land she did not know.

f.w: left thy father and thy mother, and the land of thy nativity

n: Boaz prays that the Lord will reward Ruth. He pictures her as a young bird sheltering under God's wings — a lovely image of trust and protection.

f.g: repay, reward

n: Ruth humbly thanks Boaz for comforting her and speaking kindly, even though she does not have the standing of one of his own servant girls.

f.g: Literally “spoken to the heart” — spoken kindly and reassuringly.

n: Boaz invites Ruth to eat with the workers and personally serves her roasted grain. She eats until satisfied and still has food left over to take home to Naomi.

f.g: Probably a sour wine or vinegar dip used to flavor bread.
roasted grain
satisfied, full

n: Boaz goes beyond the law's requirement, letting Ruth glean even among the bundled sheaves, normally off-limits, and telling his men not to shame her.

f.g: do not embarrass or scold her

n: He even has the workers drop extra grain on purpose for her. Generosity done quietly, without humiliating the receiver, reflects the Lord's own kindness.

f.g: on purpose, deliberately

n: Ruth works until evening and threshes her grain: about an ephah of barley, a remarkably large amount for one day of gleaning.

f.g: A dry measure of roughly 20–40 pounds of grain — perhaps weeks of food for two women.
threshed — beat the stalks to separate the grain

n: Ruth carries the grain home and also gives Naomi the leftover roasted grain from lunch. Naomi's emptiness is beginning to be filled.
Naomi is astonished at the amount and blesses whoever helped Ruth. Only at the end does Ruth reveal the man's name — Boaz — a dramatic moment in the story.

f.g: did you work

n: Naomi's bitterness softens to praise: the Lord has not stopped showing kindness to the living (Naomi and Ruth) and the dead (their husbands). She reveals Boaz is a close relative with family duties.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal covenant love.
Hebrew go'el — a kinsman-redeemer who could buy back family land, free relatives from debt, or marry a widow to preserve the family name.

n: Ruth adds that Boaz invited her to stay with his workers through the whole harvest. Her continued title “the Moabitess” reminds us she is still an outsider being welcomed in.
Naomi agrees this is wise, since in another field Ruth might be mistreated. Naomi is now actively looking out for Ruth's welfare.

f.g: The sense is “so that no one harms you.”

n: Ruth gleans with Boaz's workers through both the barley and wheat harvests — about seven weeks — while living with and caring for Naomi.

f.g: Wheat harvest ended around the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost), about seven weeks after barley harvest began.
